answer: Within the period 2000–1100 BCE, the highest-growth phase occurred in the 15th century BCE (1500–1401 BCE). In that century the kernel-density-estimation growth rate of all archaeological indicators (g_all_mean) averages +0.00283 (median +0.00290) and the pollen-openness growth rate (pollen_grate_100) averages +0.00189 (median +0.00174), giving a z-score composite of +1.20 — the highest of any century in the window; the annual peaks of both growth-rate series fall squarely inside this century (BCE 1443 for KDE growth, BCE 1415 for pollen growth). The 14th century BCE (1400–1301 BCE) is the clear second-highest growth century (g_all_mean +0.00145, pollen_grate_100 +0.00111, composite +0.67), followed by the 17th century BCE (composite +0.26); every later century (13th–11th) has negative growth. Secondary evidence corroborates but slightly lags: the capital Z-indicators show their largest single-century aggregate rise into the 14th century BCE (mean Z +0.68, led by Copper/Gold +2.90), and the pollen-openness level (MEAN and 100-yr smooth) shows its steepest forward-century rises into the 13th (and 12th) century BCE — i.e., capital build-up and pollen level-accumulation trail the growth-rate peak by roughly one century, consistent with a growth phase rooted in the 15th century BCE. Caveats: (a) the two rate series genuinely diverge in the 16th century BCE (1600–1501 BCE) — KDE growth is strongly positive (+0.00115, 100% of years positive) while pollen growth is negative (−0.00301, 0% of years positive) — so I report that divergence rather than averaging it away, which is why the 16th century ranks only mid-table; (b) the 2000–1100 BCE window maps to CE −2000…−1100 (calBP 3950–3050); (c) interpolated columns are the operative annual series because raw observations are only ~1–5% present in the window; (d) centuries use the standard 'n-th century BCE' convention (15th = 1500–1401 BCE) and the 11th-century bin contains a single in-window year (1100 BCE) due to the window edge. Conclusion: the highest growth phase of 2000–1100 BCE was the 15th century BCE, with the 14th century BCE as the strong runner-up.

payload.hypothesis: Within 2000-1100 BCE the highest growth phase was the 15th century BCE (1500-1401 BCE), with the 14th century BCE (1400-1301 BCE) as the clear second-highest growth century.
payload.workflow: 1) Load three CSVs (time_series yearly CE -4100..-500; capital century-resolution comma-decimal; pollen yearly comma-decimal), map BCE= -CE, calBP=1950-CE; restrict window 2000-1100 BCE (901 yearly rows, CE -2000..-1100; 10 century-resolution capital rows). 2) Bin years into standard n-th century BCE bins (15th = 1500-1401, etc.). 3) Aggregate the two growth-rate series g_all_mean and pollen_grate_100 per century (mean, median), build per-year z-scores over the window and a z_comp=(z_g+z_p)/2 composite, rank centuries. 4) Cross-check secondary proxies: capital mean-Z century-over-century changes and pollen MEAN/SMOOTH level forward-century rises. 5) Reconcile: rate series agree on 15th c BCE as peak; capital build-up largest into 14th c; pollen level rises lag into 13th-12th c; 16th c has KDE-positive but pollen-negative divergence (reported not averaged). Deliverable written as a natural-language hypothesis.
